name: evangelism-apologetics-and-church-planting
description: Evangelism, Apologetics, Preaching, Teaching and Church Planting: a practitioner reference for Christian ministry that treats evangelism as a communication task and then holds itself to what the evidence on communication actually supports. The persuasion findings the source stands behind -- listening first produces durable change, conversation beats broadcast, moral reframing is difficult and rarely done, relevant evidence is the strongest identified lever, facts alone against identity-linked beliefs persuade less than assumed -- read as tendencies rather than measured effects, with no number supplied because the source supplies none; trust decomposed into competence, reliability and care and why most trust failures are the third mistaken for the first; the four levels of listening, silence as the most underused technique, asking before advising, and recognising when a spiritual question has actually been asked. Six evangelistic approaches -- relational, lifestyle, missional, conversational, proclamation, service -- compared on strengths and limitations, with the limitations column read carefully because half of it is structural fact and half theological judgement held inside the source's tradition; the four common gospel presentations (the Roman Road, the Bridge to Life, the Four Spiritual Laws, Creation-Fall-Redemption-Restoration) and what each compression drops. The ethics of influence carried as load-bearing rather than as an appendix: the disclosure test -- if you told the person exactly what you were doing and why, would this still work -- the structural line between persuasion, manipulation and coercion, power asymmetry where a pastor, parent or employer holds it, exploited states, and the hard cases including altar calls, which the source does not rule on. The cosmological, teleological, moral and ontological arguments as the source gives them with the standard objection each actually faces, kept inside its own framing that the case is cumulative rather than demonstrative; the minimal-facts resurrection argument with the criticisms it actually faces and the five alternative explanations -- swoon, hallucination, legend, theft, cognitive dissonance -- tabulated rather than strengthened; the manuscript and dating case for the New Testament with transmission kept distinct from veracity; the problems of evil with the free will defense read precisely as a defense, soul-making and its limits, and the pastoral dimension; four common objections answered; and presuppositional, classical and cumulative-case method compared, with listening named the most important apologetic skill. Then the five-part sermon structure and four patterns, expository method and the curse of knowledge, delivery and speech anxiety, and the six-day rhythm ending in the one-sentence test; small-group facilitation, deciding how you will decide before discussing, wait time and question types, the four-stage discipleship process with fading guidance, the spiritual disciplines, and learning as a change in long-term memory with an honest account of how firmly each teaching claim stands; six church-planting models compared and deliberately not ranked, the five phases from assessment to post-launch, onboarding as the growth constraint, the tyranny of structurelessness, volunteer burnout as a structural problem rather than a personal weakness, the missing stair and safeguarding as a legal obligation, and the founder-to-team transition -- plus the sixteen-term glossary pointed at the section that argues each term in context, and the further reading with the note that every author on the list argues for the position.
